chunks: Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Faḍḍāl, from ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd, from Muṣaddiq ibn Ṣadaqah, from ʿAmmār al-Sābāṭī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:

He was asked about a jug or vessel that becomes filthy: how should it be washed, and how many times should it be washed? He said: “Three times: water is poured into it and swirled within it, then that water is emptied from it; then other water is poured into it and swirled within it, then that water is emptied from it; then other water is poured into it and swirled within it, then emptied from it, and it has become pure.” And about water from which a chicken has drunk, he said: “If there is filth on its beak, then do not perform wudu (ablution) from it and do not drink; but if you do not know that there is filth on its beak, then perform wudu (ablution) and drink.” And he said: “Everything whose flesh is eaten, then perform wudu (ablution) from it and drink it.” And about water from which a hawk, falcon, or eagle drinks, he said: “Everything among birds—wudu (ablution) may be performed from what it drinks from, unless you see blood on its beak; so if you see blood on its beak, then do not perform wudu (ablution) from it and do not drink.” And he said: “Wash the vessel in which you find a dead rat seven times.”

And he was asked about a well into which a dog, mouse, or pig falls. He said: “All of it is to be drained; but if the water overcomes that, then let it be drained for a day until the night, then a group of people should stand over it taking turns two by two, draining it for a day until the night, and it has become pure.” And he was asked about a dog and a mouse when they eat from bread and the like. He said: “Part of it is to be discarded, and the remainder eaten.” And he was asked about cow urine that a man drinks. He said: “If he is in need of it and seeks treatment with it, he may drink it; and likewise the urine of camels and sheep.”

And about flour in which mouse droppings fall—whether eating it is permissible—he said: “If some of it remains, there is no harm; its upper part is taken and thrown away.” And he was asked about the beetle, the fly, the locust, the ant, and the like, when they die in a well, oil, clarified butter, and the like. He said: “Everything that has no blood, there is no harm in it.” And about a lizard falling into milk, he said: “The milk becomes forbidden.” And he said: “Indeed, there is poison in it.”
And he said: “Everything is clean until you know that it is filthy; so when you know, then it has indeed become filthy; and whatever you do not know, there is nothing upon you regarding it.”

key_terms.اللَّبَنُ: milk, discussed here in relation to contamination
key_terms.الْجُرَذَ: the rat or large mouse found dead in a vessel
key_terms.تُنْزَفُ: it is to be drained out, especially regarding a well
key_terms.خُرْءُ: droppings or excrement, here of a mouse
key_terms.طَهُرَ: became pure after prescribed washing or cleansing
key_terms.قَذِرٌ: filthy or impure in the context of najasah
key_terms.نَظِيفٌ: clean, pure, and not judged impure

ai.seo_question: What does the hadith say about ritual purity, impure vessels, contaminated water, and the principle that everything is clean until proven filthy?
ai.summary: This hadith gathers a series of legal rulings on taharah (ritual purity), najasah, and the use of water, vessels, food, and other substances that may come into contact with impurities. It establishes practical rules for washing impure containers, judging water used by animals, handling contamination in wells and foods, and concludes with the foundational principle that things are considered clean unless their impurity becomes known.
